source.name: ASTRA chemistry practice set
source.license: Original syllabus-based practice questions (exam-frequent themes; not verbatim past papers)

questions.stem: Dobereiner arranged chemically similar elements into sets of three that he called
questions.explanation: Each Dobereiner triad contains three related elements, with the middle one intermediate in properties.

questions.stem: In a Dobereiner triad the atomic mass of the middle element is approximately
options: the product of the other two atomic masses
the arithmetic mean of the other two atomic masses
twice the atomic mass of the lightest member
equal to the atomic number of the heaviest member
questions.explanation: The middle atomic mass is close to the average of the first and third members.

questions.stem: Newlands noticed that every eighth element resembled the first and named this regularity the
questions.explanation: He compared the repeating chemical likeness to the octaves of a musical scale.

questions.stem: Newlands' arrangement gave a useful resemblance of properties only as far as the element
questions.explanation: Beyond calcium the octave pattern broke down as many new elements were fitted in.

questions.stem: Mendeleev's periodic law stated that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their
questions.explanation: Mendeleev ordered the then-known elements by increasing atomic mass and found a repeating pattern.

questions.stem: A distinctive feature of Mendeleev's table was that he
options: left vacant places for elements still undiscovered
arranged elements strictly by atomic number
refused to predict any new element
questions.explanation: Gaps such as those for eka-aluminium and eka-silicon were later filled by gallium and germanium.

questions.stem: A recognised limitation of Mendeleev's classification is the uncertain position of
questions.explanation: Isotopes have different atomic masses but identical chemistry, so a mass-based table cannot place them uniquely.

questions.stem: The element Mendeleev called eka-aluminium was later isolated and named
questions.explanation: Eka-aluminium occupies the place under aluminium and matches gallium in properties and atomic mass.

questions.stem: Eka-silicon of Mendeleev's table corresponds to the later-discovered element
questions.explanation: Germanium fills the gap Mendeleev left beneath silicon and agrees with his predicted properties.

questions.stem: Tellurium was placed before iodine in Mendeleev's table even though Te has the greater atomic mass so that
options: tellurium would sit with the noble gases
chemically similar elements remained in the same group
iodine would have a lower atomic number
the table would contain only eight periods
questions.explanation: Chemical analogy (Te with O, S, Se; I with F, Cl, Br) was given priority over a strict mass sequence.

questions.stem: In the triad lithium–sodium–potassium the atomic mass of sodium is close to
options: the difference of the atomic masses of Li and K
the mean of the atomic masses of lithium and potassium
twice the atomic mass of potassium
questions.explanation: Li (7), Na (23) and K (39) illustrate Dobereiner's mean-mass rule for a triad.

questions.stem: Argon (atomic mass about 40) sits before potassium (about 39) in the older table because
options: argon has the smaller atomic number, which Mendeleev already used
chemical properties forced the placement; atomic number later justified it
argon has fewer neutrons than potassium
questions.explanation: Mass inversion of the Ar–K pair is an anomalous pair of Mendeleev's table, resolved by Moseley's atomic-number order.

questions.stem: The modern periodic law states that properties of elements are a periodic function of their
questions.explanation: After Moseley, atomic number Z replaced atomic mass as the classifying index.

questions.stem: Henry Moseley's X-ray studies showed that the correct basis for classifying elements is
questions.explanation: The frequency of characteristic X-rays varies regularly with Z, not with A.

questions.stem: The long form of the periodic table is constructed primarily on the basis of
questions.explanation: Each period begins when a new principal shell starts to fill and ends at a noble-gas configuration.

questions.stem: In the long form of the periodic table the number of vertical groups is
questions.explanation: IUPAC numbers the groups from 1 to 18 in the 18-column table.

questions.stem: The long form of the periodic table contains how many horizontal periods?
questions.explanation: Periods 1 to 7 run from hydrogen to the heaviest known elements.

questions.stem: A horizontal row of the periodic table is called a
questions.explanation: Elements in one period have the same valence principal quantum number.

questions.stem: A vertical column of the periodic table is called a
questions.explanation: A group collects elements with the same valence-shell configuration and similar chemistry.

questions.stem: Elements of one group show similar chemical properties mainly because they have
questions.explanation: Valence configuration repeats down a group (for example ns¹ for alkali metals).

questions.stem: The period number of an element equals the
options: principal quantum number of its valence shell
questions.explanation: Period 3 elements have n = 3 as the outer shell, period 4 have n = 4, and so on.

questions.stem: IUPAC temporary names for elements with Z greater than 100 are built from
options: Latin roots of the digits of the atomic number
the atomic mass rounded to an integer
the name of the mineral in which they occur
questions.explanation: Each digit 0–9 has a Latin stem (nil, un, bi, …) so Z = 107 is unnilseptium until a permanent name is approved.

questions.stem: Isotopes of one element occupy a single position in the modern table because they share the
questions.explanation: The modern law uses Z; isotopes differ in N and A but not in Z or chemistry.

questions.stem: The argon–potassium pair is placed in the order Ar then K once elements are arranged by
questions.explanation: Z(Ar) = 18 and Z(K) = 19, so the modern sequence matches chemical groups even though A(Ar) > A(K).

questions.stem: A group-2 (alkaline earth) atom has how many valence electrons in the ns subshell?
questions.explanation: The configuration ends in ns², so the group number in the s-block equals the valence-electron count.

questions.stem: Lanthanoids and actinoids are written as two separate rows beneath the main table so that
options: they are excluded from the periodic law
they can be treated as noble gases
their atomic numbers can be ignored
questions.explanation: Inserting fourteen extra cells into periods 6 and 7 would make those rows awkwardly wide.

questions.stem: The fourteen lanthanoids still belong chemically to which period of the long form table?
questions.explanation: They follow lanthanum in period 6; actinoids similarly belong to period 7.

questions.stem: Moseley found that the square root of the characteristic X-ray frequency varies linearly with atomic number as $\sqrt{\nu}=a(Z-b)$. This showed that
options: atomic mass is still the fundamental index
Z, not A, is the property that orders the elements
X-rays arise from valence-shell jumps only
questions.explanation: A plot of $\sqrt{\nu}$ against Z is a straight line; plots against atomic mass are irregular, so Z is the true periodic argument.

questions.stem: Alkali metals and alkaline earth metals together constitute the
questions.explanation: Their differentiating electron enters the ns subshell (groups 1 and 2).

questions.stem: The p-block of the long form table begins at boron and ends at
options: the noble gases of each period
questions.explanation: Groups 13–18 are p-block; the last member of each of these periods is a noble gas.

questions.stem: d-block elements are those whose differentiating electron enters a
questions.explanation: That is the definition of the transition series occupying groups 3–12.

questions.stem: Lanthanoids and actinoids together constitute the
questions.explanation: Their differentiating electron enters the (n−2)f subshell; they are the inner transition elements.

questions.stem: Hydrogen and helium are the only two members of the
questions.explanation: Period 1 fills the 1s subshell and therefore contains just H and He.

questions.stem: A short period of eight members starts at lithium and ends at
questions.explanation: Period 2 fills 2s and 2p (2 + 6 = 8 elements) from Li to Ne.

questions.stem: Sodium through argon form the second short period, matching the length of the
questions.explanation: Period 3 also has eight elements (3s and 3p); 3d is not yet available.

questions.stem: Filling of 4s, 3d and 4p subshells produces the first long period of
questions.explanation: 2 + 10 + 6 = 18 elements from potassium to krypton.

questions.stem: Group 1 elements other than hydrogen are collectively called
questions.explanation: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs and Fr are the alkali metals.

questions.stem: Beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium and radium are the
questions.explanation: They form group 2 and have the valence configuration ns².

questions.stem: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine belong to the
questions.explanation: Group 17 elements are the halogens (salt-formers).

questions.stem: Neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon occupy the
options: last vertical column of the long form table
questions.explanation: They are the noble gases of group 18 (helium is also placed there).

questions.stem: Main-group (representative) elements are those belonging to the
questions.explanation: s- and p-block elements have their last electron in an ns or np orbital and show the classic group valences.

questions.stem: An element is classed as a transition metal if it has an incomplete d subshell in the
options: free atom or in any of its common ions
questions.explanation: IUPAC uses the incomplete-(n−1)d criterion; Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰) is often set aside as a typical transition ion.

questions.stem: Inner transition metals are distinguished from the d-block by the filling of an
questions.explanation: Lanthanoids fill 4f and actinoids fill 5f, so they are the f-block (inner transition) series.

questions.stem: Including the fourteen lanthanoids, the sixth period contains
questions.explanation: Period 6 fills 6s, 4f, 5d and 6p: 2 + 14 + 10 + 6 = 32.

questions.stem: Boron heads group 13; the remaining members of that group are best described as
questions.explanation: Al, Ga, In and Tl are metals; boron is the non-metallic/metalloid head of the group.

questions.stem: Helium is placed with the noble gases even though its configuration is $1s^{2}$ because
options: it has an incomplete p subshell
it has a closed shell and is chemically inert
questions.explanation: A filled 1s shell gives helium the noble-gas chemistry of group 18, not the s-block reactivity of group 2.

questions.stem: The fourth period contains eighteen elements because the subshells that fill in that period are
questions.explanation: Capacity 2 + 10 + 6 = 18; 4f is not occupied until period 6.

questions.stem: The f-block is printed below the main table because inserting the fourteen lanthanoids into period 6 would
questions.explanation: The two-row footnote is a display convention; chemically the lanthanoids still belong in period 6.

questions.stem: On moving from left to right across a period, the atomic radius of the elements generally
questions.explanation: Rising effective nuclear charge pulls the same-shell electrons inward, so the atom shrinks.

questions.stem: On descending a group, the atomic radius of the elements generally
options: is independent of the new shell
questions.explanation: Each step down adds a principal shell, which outweighs the extra nuclear charge.

questions.stem: A cation is always smaller than the parent atom from which it is formed because
options: electrons are lost and the remaining cloud is held more tightly
questions.explanation: Fewer electrons and a higher Zeff/electron ratio contract the ion relative to the atom.

questions.stem: An anion is always larger than the parent atom from which it is formed because
options: extra electrons raise inter-electronic repulsion and the cloud expands
the ion has fewer electrons than the atom
questions.explanation: The added electron(s) swell the electron cloud, so r(anion) > r(atom).

questions.stem: The covalent radius of an atom is half the internuclear distance in a
options: van der Waals contact between two non-bonded atoms
questions.explanation: In Cl₂, for example, r(cov) = ½ d(Cl–Cl).

questions.stem: For the same element the van der Waals radius compared with the covalent radius is
questions.explanation: van der Waals contact is a non-bonded approach, so the apparent radius is greater than the bonded covalent radius.

questions.stem: The steady rise of effective nuclear charge across a period pulls the electron cloud inward and therefore
questions.explanation: Zeff increases left to right while n stays the same, so atomic size falls.

questions.stem: Addition of a new principal shell is the main reason atomic size
questions.explanation: The extra shell lies farther from the nucleus, so group radii increase top to bottom.

questions.stem: Metallic radius is half the distance between neighbouring nuclei in a
questions.explanation: It is the radius used for metals in the close-packed or body-centred lattice.

questions.stem: Isoelectronic species are atoms or ions that contain
questions.explanation: N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ are a familiar isoelectronic set (10 electrons).

questions.stem: In an isoelectronic series the ionic radius falls as the
questions.explanation: More protons pull the same number of electrons more tightly, so size decreases with Z.

questions.stem: The fluoride ion is larger than a neutral fluorine atom because of
questions.explanation: Adding one electron to F expands the 2p cloud, so r(F⁻) > r(F).

questions.stem: Sodium ion is smaller than a sodium atom because
options: the entire 3s electron has been removed
nuclear charge of Na⁺ is smaller
questions.explanation: Na is [Ne] 3s¹; Na⁺ is a compact neon-like core with higher Zeff per electron.

questions.stem: Among Li, Na, K and Rb, the atom with the largest covalent radius is
questions.explanation: Size increases down group 1 as extra shells are added; Rb is the heaviest of the four.

questions.stem: Among Na, Mg, Al and Si, the smallest atomic radius belongs to
questions.explanation: Across period 3, Zeff rises and size falls, so Si is the smallest of this set.

questions.stem: The correct order of ionic radii is
questions.explanation: These four ions are isoelectronic (10 e⁻); radius falls as Z rises from 8 (O) to 12 (Mg).

questions.stem: Gallium has an atomic radius close to that of aluminium because of
options: a sudden drop in nuclear charge
questions.explanation: Poorly shielding 3d¹⁰ electrons raise Zeff on Ga and cancel the expected size increase down the group.

questions.stem: Among the isoelectronic set S²⁻, Cl⁻, K⁺ and Ca²⁺, the smallest species is
questions.explanation: All have 18 electrons; Ca²⁺ has the largest nuclear charge (Z = 20) and therefore the most contracted cloud.

questions.stem: The covalent radius of silicon is larger than that of carbon because silicon
options: has a greater Zeff in the same shell
questions.explanation: C is period 2 and Si is period 3; the added n = 3 shell makes Si larger.

questions.stem: The size order Li⁺ > Be²⁺ > B³⁺ holds because
options: electron count rises along the series
nuclear charge rises while the electron count stays two
a new shell is added at each step
questions.explanation: All three are 1s² species; higher Z pulls the same two electrons closer.

questions.stem: Zirconium and hafnium have nearly identical atomic radii because of
options: a fall in Z from Zr to Hf
questions.explanation: The 14 poorly shielding 4f electrons inserted before Hf shrink it so that r(Hf) ≈ r(Zr).

questions.stem: Fe²⁺ is larger than Fe³⁺ because removal of an extra electron
options: raises Zeff and shrinks the remaining 3d cloud
converts iron into a noble gas
questions.explanation: Both ions are iron, but Fe³⁺ has fewer electrons and a higher charge density, so it is the smaller cation.

questions.stem: Ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its
questions.explanation: The textbook definition uses the ground-state gaseous atom: M(g) → M⁺(g) + e⁻.

questions.stem: The first ionisation enthalpy refers to removal of an electron from the
questions.explanation: IE₁ is for M(g); IE₂ is for M⁺(g), and so on.

questions.stem: First ionisation enthalpy generally increases from left to right across a
questions.explanation: Zeff rises and size falls across a period, so the outer electron is harder to remove.

questions.stem: First ionisation enthalpy generally decreases from top to bottom in a
questions.explanation: The valence electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded in the heavier congener.

questions.stem: Ionisation enthalpies of elements are commonly expressed in
questions.explanation: TSBIE tables quote ΔᵢH in kJ mol⁻¹ (sometimes also in eV per atom).

questions.stem: Noble gases have exceptionally high ionisation enthalpies because of their
questions.explanation: A complete ns² np⁶ (or 1s² for He) set is especially stable, so removal of an electron costs a lot of energy.

questions.stem: In any period the alkali metal has the
options: same IE as the noble gas
questions.explanation: The single ns¹ electron is large, weakly held and easily lost.

questions.stem: The second ionisation enthalpy of an element compared with its first is always
questions.explanation: The second electron is taken from a already positive ion, so IE₂ > IE₁ in every case.

questions.stem: Metals typically have lower ionisation enthalpies than the non-metals of the
questions.explanation: Left-hand (metallic) elements are larger and have smaller Zeff, so they lose electrons more readily.

questions.stem: Inner-electron screening reduces the effective nuclear charge and thereby
questions.explanation: A well-shielded valence electron feels less pull and is easier to remove.

questions.stem: A smaller atomic radius generally corresponds to a
questions.explanation: The outer electron is closer to the nucleus and more tightly bound in a smaller atom.

questions.stem: Successive ionisation enthalpies of an atom increase because the cation left behind
options: holds its remaining electrons more tightly
questions.explanation: Each removal raises the charge on the ion and shrinks the cloud, so the next IE is larger.

questions.stem: The process whose enthalpy change is the first ionisation enthalpy is
questions.explanation: IE₁ is defined for the isolated gaseous atom losing one electron.

questions.stem: Among the period-2 elements, the highest first ionisation enthalpy belongs to
questions.explanation: Neon is the noble gas of that period and has the most tightly held closed-shell electrons.

questions.stem: Beryllium has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than boron because Be has a
questions.explanation: Removing an electron from stable 2s² (Be) costs more than removing the single 2p electron of B.

questions.stem: Nitrogen has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than oxygen because N has a
questions.explanation: The extra stability of half-filled 2p³ outweighs the one-unit rise in Z from N to O.

questions.stem: Magnesium shows a higher first ionisation enthalpy than aluminium, an exception similar to
questions.explanation: Mg (3s²) is harder to ionise than Al (3p¹), just as Be (2s²) is harder than B (2p¹).

questions.stem: Phosphorus has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than sulphur because of the extra stability of the
questions.explanation: P is 3p³; the paired 3p⁴ electron of S is easier to remove, so IE(P) > IE(S).

questions.stem: Between lithium and beryllium, beryllium has the greater first ionisation enthalpy because of its
questions.explanation: Be is smaller, has one extra proton and a filled 2s pair, so IE₁(Be) > IE₁(Li).

questions.stem: The second ionisation enthalpy of sodium is very large because the second electron must be taken from the
questions.explanation: After loss of 3s¹, Na⁺ is isoelectronic with Ne; breaking that closed shell requires a large IE₂.

questions.stem: First ionisation enthalpy falls in the order Li > Na > K because
options: nuclear charge falls down the group
atomic size increases down the group
the number of valence electrons increases
questions.explanation: The ns¹ electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded in Na and K than in Li.

questions.stem: Although oxygen has a higher nuclear charge than nitrogen, its first ionisation enthalpy is lower because
options: oxygen has the larger atomic radius
the extra electron in 2p⁴ is paired and is easier to remove
questions.explanation: Size would suggest IE(O) > IE(N), but pairing repulsion in 2p⁴ reverses the trend.

questions.stem: Boron has a lower first ionisation enthalpy than beryllium even though B is smaller, because
options: the 2p electron of B is shielded by 2s² and is easier to remove than a 2s electron of Be
nuclear charge falls from Be to B
questions.explanation: The two trends conflict: smaller size would raise IE, but the change of subshell (2s → 2p) lowers it, and the subshell effect wins.

questions.stem: For magnesium, the jump between IE₂ and IE₃ is much larger than between IE₁ and IE₂ because the third electron
questions.explanation: Mg is 3s², so IE₁ and IE₂ remove valence electrons; IE₃ must break the 2p⁶ core and is therefore very large.

questions.stem: Electron gain enthalpy is the enthalpy change when an electron is added to a neutral gaseous atom to form a
questions.explanation: The defining process is X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g); ΔegH is usually negative when energy is released.

questions.stem: A more negative electron gain enthalpy means a greater tendency of the atom to
questions.explanation: The more energy released on adding an electron, the more favourable the gain.

questions.stem: Halogens have the most negative electron gain enthalpies in their respective periods because they
options: are one electron short of a noble-gas configuration
are the largest atoms of the period
questions.explanation: Adding one electron completes ns² np⁶ and releases a large amount of energy.

questions.stem: Noble-gas atoms have positive electron gain enthalpies because the extra electron must
options: pair in a half-filled p set
questions.explanation: The incoming electron is added to a higher-n orbital against a closed shell, so energy must be supplied.

questions.stem: Electron gain enthalpy generally becomes more negative on moving from left to right in a
questions.explanation: Zeff rises and the vacancy is closer to the nucleus, so electron attachment is more exothermic.

questions.stem: On moving down a halogen group, electron gain enthalpy generally becomes less negative after
questions.explanation: Cl has the most negative value; Br and I are less exothermic as the added electron is farther from the nucleus.

questions.stem: Among the first two halogens, the more negative electron gain enthalpy belongs to
questions.explanation: Cl is more exothermic than F, a well-known exception to the simple down-group trend.

questions.stem: The second electron gain enthalpy of an atom is always
questions.explanation: A negative ion must accept another electron, so energy is required and ΔegH₂ > 0.

questions.stem: Conversion of O⁻(g) to O²⁻(g) is endothermic because a negative ion must
options: accept another electron against its own charge
questions.explanation: Electron–electron repulsion in O⁻ makes the second attachment unfavourable; oxides form in the lattice, not as free O²⁻(g).

questions.stem: Electron affinity is often quoted as the negative of the
questions.explanation: Many older tables list EA as a positive number equal to −ΔegH when attachment is exothermic.

questions.stem: Fluorine has a less negative electron gain enthalpy than chlorine because the compact 2p cloud of F suffers
options: strong electron–electron repulsion when an extra electron is added
questions.explanation: The incoming electron is forced into a very small 2p orbital already crowded with electrons.

questions.stem: Among F, Cl, Br and I, the most negative electron gain enthalpy belongs to
questions.explanation: Chlorine combines a high Zeff with a large enough 3p orbital to avoid the extreme repulsion seen in F.

questions.stem: Nitrogen has a near-zero or slightly positive electron gain enthalpy because its 2p subshell is already
questions.explanation: Adding an electron to 2p³ forces pairing and destroys the half-filled stability, so attachment is unfavourable.

questions.stem: Beryllium and magnesium have unfavourable (near-zero or positive) electron gain enthalpies because they possess
questions.explanation: The extra electron would have to enter a higher np orbital against a closed s pair.

questions.stem: Among carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine, the most negative electron gain enthalpy is that of
questions.explanation: Fluorine is one electron short of neon and, despite the F/Cl anomaly, is still the most exothermic of this period-2 set.

questions.stem: Chlorine outruns fluorine in electron gain enthalpy because the incoming electron enters a larger 3p orbital with less repulsion, even though fluorine has the
questions.explanation: Two trends compete: F is smaller and more electronegative, yet inter-electronic repulsion in the compact 2p cloud makes ΔegH(F) less negative than ΔegH(Cl).

questions.stem: Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a chemical bond to attract the
questions.explanation: It is a bonded-atom property, not an isolated-atom energy.

questions.stem: The most widely used numerical scale of electronegativity is the
questions.explanation: Pauling assigned fluorine the value 4.0 and built the rest of the scale from bond-energy data.

questions.stem: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, with a Pauling value of about
questions.explanation: χ(F) = 4.0 is the reference maximum on the Pauling scale.

questions.stem: Electronegativity of representative elements generally increases from left to right across a
questions.explanation: Zeff rises and size falls, so the bonded atom pulls the shared pair more strongly.

questions.stem: Electronegativity of representative elements generally decreases from top to bottom in a
questions.explanation: The bonding electrons are farther from the nucleus in the heavier congener.

questions.stem: Among the alkali metals, the member with a particularly low electronegativity is
questions.explanation: Cs is large and weakly attracting; it is one of the most electropositive metals.

questions.stem: Electronegativity is a bonding property of an atom in a molecule, not an isolated-atom energy like
questions.explanation: IE and electron gain enthalpy refer to gaseous atoms or ions; χ is defined for an atom already in a bond.

questions.stem: A large electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms favours
questions.explanation: The shared pair is strongly displaced toward the more electronegative atom, approaching ion formation.

questions.stem: After fluorine, the next most electronegative element is
questions.explanation: Pauling values: F (4.0) > O (3.5) > N ≈ Cl (about 3.0).

questions.stem: Metals are characterised by low electronegativity values compared with
questions.explanation: Low χ and low IE together describe the electropositive, electron-losing behaviour of metals.

questions.stem: Electronegativity falls in the order N > P > As because
options: nuclear charge falls down the group
the number of valence electrons decreases
questions.explanation: The bonded pair is held farther from the nucleus in the larger P and As atoms.

questions.stem: In period 2 the electronegativity order is
questions.explanation: χ rises steadily across the period as Zeff increases and radius falls.

questions.stem: Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, bromine and iodine because of its
options: small size and high effective nuclear charge
questions.explanation: The shared pair in an F–X bond sits closest to a compact, highly charged fluorine atom.

questions.stem: On the Mulliken scale, electronegativity is taken as the average of
options: ionisation enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy (in suitable units)
questions.explanation: Mulliken wrote χ ∝ (IE + EA)/2, combining the two isolated-atom energies that measure electron holding and accepting.

questions.stem: The H–F bond is more polar than the H–Cl bond because fluorine is
questions.explanation: The greater χ(F) − χ(H) gap displaces the shared pair more strongly toward fluorine.

questions.stem: Fluorine outranks chlorine in electronegativity even though Cl has more protons, because the bonding pair in an F–X bond is
options: much closer to the small, poorly shielded fluorine atom
questions.explanation: Size and Zeff on the valence shell dominate χ; the extra protons of Cl are offset by an extra shielding shell.

questions.stem: Valence electrons of an atom are those present in its
questions.explanation: Chemical valence is decided by the electrons in the highest principal shell.

questions.stem: Alkali metals exhibit a characteristic valence of
questions.explanation: Each atom has a single ns¹ electron, which it loses (or shares) in compounds.

questions.stem: Halogens commonly exhibit a valence of one, corresponding to the oxidation state
questions.explanation: Gain of one electron completes the octet and gives X⁻ (fluoride, chloride, …).

questions.stem: The characteristic oxidation state of alkali metals in their compounds is
questions.explanation: Loss of the single valence electron leaves a noble-gas cation M⁺.

questions.stem: For many p-block elements the highest oxidation state equals the
options: number of valence electrons (the old group number)
questions.explanation: Group 15 can reach +5, group 16 +6 and group 17 +7 when all valence electrons are involved.

questions.stem: Carbon is tetravalent in the great majority of its stable compounds because it has
questions.explanation: The 2s² 2p² set provides four electrons for four covalent bonds (as in CH₄).

questions.stem: Transition metals are noted for showing
questions.explanation: Both ns and (n−1)d electrons can take part in bonding, so several OS are common.

questions.stem: In most of its compounds oxygen exhibits the oxidation state
questions.explanation: Oxygen is highly electronegative and usually completes its octet by gaining or sharing two electrons.

questions.stem: Nitrogen can show oxidation states ranging from −3 in ammonia to +5 in
questions.explanation: HNO₃ and nitrates use all five valence electrons of N; NH₃ uses the −3 state.

questions.stem: Manganese attains its highest oxidation state of +7 in the
questions.explanation: In MnO₄⁻ the seven 4s and 3d electrons of Mn are all involved in bonding.

questions.stem: Sulphur can show the +6 state in SO₃, whereas oxygen rarely exceeds −2, because sulphur has
questions.explanation: The 3d orbitals of S allow expansion of the octet; second-period O cannot do this.

questions.stem: Chlorine exhibits odd positive oxidation states +1, +3, +5 and +7 in addition to
questions.explanation: The −1 state is the halide; the odd positive states appear in oxoacids and oxides as 3s and 3p (and 3d) electrons are unpaired.

questions.stem: Group-14 elements typically form tetravalent compounds, matching
questions.explanation: The valence configuration ns² np² supplies four electrons for four bonds (CCl₄, SiCl₄, …).

questions.stem: Among the 3d metals, the highest oxidation state is +7, shown by manganese, equal to the total of its
questions.explanation: Mn is 4s² 3d⁵; using all seven electrons gives Mn(VII) as in KMnO₄. Iron does not reach +8 in ordinary compounds.

questions.stem: Metallic character of elements increases on moving
options: across a period from left to right
questions.explanation: Size grows and IE falls down a group, so the atom loses electrons more readily.

questions.stem: Metallic character of elements decreases on moving from left to right across a
questions.explanation: IE and electronegativity rise across a period, so electron loss becomes less favourable.

questions.stem: Metals tend to lose valence electrons and form
questions.explanation: Electropositive behaviour is the chemical signature of metallic character.

questions.stem: Non-metals tend to gain electrons and form anions or

questions.stem: Metallic character in the set Na, Mg, Al decreases from
questions.explanation: Across period 3 the atoms become smaller and harder to ionise, so metallic character falls Na > Mg > Al.

questions.stem: Among Li, Na and K, potassium is the most metallic because it has the
options: largest size and the lowest ionisation enthalpy
questions.explanation: Down group 1, size rises and IE falls, so K loses its 4s electron most readily of the three.

questions.explanation: Li and Mg have similar charge-to-radius ratios, so their oxides, fluorides and carbonates behave alike.

questions.stem: Silicon is classified as a metalloid, sitting on the diagonal staircase of the
questions.explanation: Si lies between the metal Al and the non-metal P and shows intermediate electrical and chemical behaviour.

questions.stem: Caesium is more metallic than lithium because the valence electron of Cs is
options: closer to the nucleus and harder to lose
farther from the nucleus and more easily lost
part of a filled p⁶ set
questions.explanation: The 6s electron of Cs is highly shielded, so Cs has a very low IE and extreme metallic character.

questions.stem: Aluminium is distinctly more metallic than boron, even though both head group 13, because Al is
options: smaller and has a higher ionisation enthalpy
larger and has a much lower ionisation enthalpy
questions.explanation: Two trends reinforce: down the group size rises and IE falls, turning the head (B, a non-metal/metalloid) into a metal (Al).

questions.stem: The first element of a p-block or s-block group differs markedly from the
questions.explanation: Li, Be, B, C, N, O and F are the classic anomalous first members.

questions.stem: The anomalous behaviour of the first element is largely due to its
questions.explanation: A compact valence shell and high χ (and IE) set the head element apart from its congeners.

questions.stem: Second-period elements lack vacant d orbitals, so they cannot
options: expand their octet the way heavier congeners can
questions.explanation: N, O and F are limited to an octet; P, S and Cl can use 3d orbitals in PF₅, SF₆, ClF₃, and so on.

questions.stem: Lithium differs from the rest of the alkali metals in several properties, including the low solubility of its
questions.explanation: LiF and Li₂CO₃ resemble the corresponding magnesium salts more than those of Na or K.

questions.stem: Lithium shows a diagonal relationship with
questions.explanation: The Li–Mg pair is the textbook diagonal relationship of group 1 / group 2.

questions.stem: Beryllium and aluminium form a well-known
questions.explanation: Be and Al share amphoteric oxides, covalent chlorides and a similar charge-to-radius ratio.

questions.stem: Hydrogen bonding is important for the hydrides of nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine, the smallest and most electronegative
questions.explanation: Only N, O and F are small and electronegative enough for strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: Lithium burns in air to give mainly the monoxide Li₂O, whereas sodium readily forms the
questions.explanation: The small Li⁺ ion is stabilised by the small O²⁻ ion; larger Na⁺ prefers the peroxide O₂²⁻.

questions.stem: Carbon–carbon single bonds are much stronger than silicon–silicon bonds, so catenation is far more characteristic of
questions.explanation: The short, strong C–C bond and the inability of C to use d orbitals make long carbon chains uniquely stable.

questions.stem: Boron forms electron-deficient compounds such as B₂H₆, a behaviour not typical of
options: aluminium alkyls in the same simple way
questions.explanation: Tiny boron has fewer valence orbitals than it needs for ordinary 2c–2e bonds, so it uses 3c–2e bridges.

questions.stem: Fluorine shows only the −1 oxidation state in its compounds, whereas chlorine can show
questions.explanation: F is the most electronegative element and has no vacant d orbitals, so it never takes a positive OS.

questions.explanation: The two ions polarise anions strongly, so their oxides, fluorides and organometallic compounds look alike — the diagonal relationship.

questions.stem: Periodicity of properties arises because similar valence-shell configurations recur at regular intervals of
questions.explanation: Each time a given ns / np pattern repeats, the chemistry of that group reappears.

questions.explanation: Inner electrons cancel part of Z; the remainder is the effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electron.

questions.stem: Inner electrons shield valence electrons from the full attraction of the
questions.explanation: Screening (shielding) is the reason Zeff is smaller than Z.

questions.stem: Effective nuclear charge felt by the outermost electron
questions.explanation: Electrons are added to the same shell, which screens poorly, so Zeff climbs left to right.

questions.explanation: The net result is a larger, more loosely held valence electron in the heavier congener.

questions.explanation: The outer electron is closer to the nucleus and harder to remove in the smaller atom.

questions.stem: Non-metallic character increases from left to right across a
questions.explanation: IE and electronegativity rise, so the tendency to gain or share electrons grows.

questions.stem: Melting points, boiling points and densities of elements also display
options: a linear fall with mass number only
questions.explanation: These bulk properties repeat in a rough pattern because bonding type and size are themselves periodic.

questions.stem: s-block elements are strongly electropositive metals, except for
questions.explanation: H and He are non-metals placed in period 1; the rest of the s-block are typical metals.

questions.stem: The p-block is the only block that contains metals, metalloids and non-metals in the
questions.explanation: Group 14, for example, runs from non-metal C through metalloid Si/Ge to metals Sn and Pb.

questions.stem: Screening of the nuclear charge is poorer by d and f electrons than by
options: s and p electrons of the same shell
questions.explanation: Penetrating s (and p) electrons cancel Z more effectively; d and f electrons leave a higher Zeff on the outside.

questions.stem: Neon has both a very small covalent radius and the highest first ionisation enthalpy of
questions.explanation: Closed-shell compactness and maximum Zeff in that row make Ne the extreme of both trends.

questions.stem: From lithium to caesium, ionisation enthalpy falls while atomic radius rises, so the two trends reinforce the
questions.explanation: A larger, more loosely held ns¹ electron makes the heavier alkali metal more metallic.

questions.stem: Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, yet chlorine has the more negative electron gain enthalpy — a pair of trends that
questions.explanation: χ follows size/Zeff, while ΔegH of F is reduced by 2p–2p repulsion; the two properties therefore order F and Cl differently.

questions.stem: Na⁺ and neon are isoelectronic, but Na⁺ has the higher ionisation enthalpy because of its
questions.explanation: Both have 10 electrons; Z(Na⁺) = 11 > Z(Ne) = 10, so the Na⁺ cloud is more tightly bound.

questions.stem: The first ionisation enthalpy of gallium is slightly higher than that of aluminium because the poorly shielding 3d¹⁰ electrons
options: turn Ga into an alkali metal
questions.explanation: d-block contraction increases Zeff and offsets the expected fall of IE down group 13.

questions.stem: Oxygen is smaller than nitrogen, which would suggest a higher IE for O, yet IE of O is lower than that of N because
options: the paired 2p⁴ electron of oxygen is easier to remove
nitrogen has the larger nuclear charge
questions.explanation: The size trend and the pairing-repulsion trend oppose each other; pairing wins, so IE(N) > IE(O).

questions.stem: Size decreases from Be to B, which would suggest a higher IE for B; the observed lower IE of B is due to
options: the ease of removing the 2p electron compared with Be 2s²
a fall in nuclear charge from Be to B
questions.explanation: Again two trends conflict: smaller radius would raise IE, but the change of subshell (2s → 2p) lowers it.
